Logical Time

Target system is made up of a (static) set of n processes each placed on different nodes

  • the model will assume that just some of them will start executing

Nodes are connected by channels. The execution can be modeled by a sequence of events → single computation that the process execute

  1. Internal Events: state changes
  1. Communication Events: send/receive of a message

Each single process is sequential → the events in a single process are totally ordered (one processor for process)

  • the k-th event executed by process pi p_ipi​﻿ is indicated as eike_i^keik​﻿
  • Sequence of all the events executed by a process ordered is named history hi:ei1,ei2,ei3,…h_i : e_i^1, e_i^2, e_i^3, \dotshi​:ei1​,ei2​,ei3​,…﻿
  • Prefix of a process history corresponds to a progression point in the local execution

I can define an order of related events for the message m in asynchronous communication:

  • send(m) happens before receive(m)
    • in synchronous communications (rendez-vous) the two events are considered to logically happen at the same time

Space-Time Diagrams

A line represent the timeline of a process

  • dots are events
  • the one with an arrows are communication events

Consistent Cuts

A set of prefixes for all process hystories is named cut

  • The set of last events for each process in a cut is called cut frontier
  • A consistent cut is the notion of a “possible progression point” of a whole distributed system → for any message m such that receive(m) is in the cut then send(m) belongs to the cut as well
    • simple mathematical way to represent causality

An ordering among cuts is induced by set inclusion relation

Some cuts cannot be ordered

No global time clock exists in a distributed system

  • I must accept some tollerance because sending messagges takes time
  • Need to understand how to relate events executed at different progression points (because there isn’t any timestap I can’t say what happens before)

Logical Time

The flow of control is described by the precedence relations among its events

  • substitute the global time
  • Precendences can express the notion of potential causality (events that happens before may have influence on what happens after)

Happens Before

Single relation defined to account for all precendes through the execution.

It has the following properties:

  1. Transitivity: three events e, f and g, if e→HBfe \xrightarrow{\text{HB}} feHB​f﻿ and f→HBgf \xrightarrow{\text{HB}} gfHB​g﻿ then e→HBge\xrightarrow{\text{HB}}geHB​g﻿
  1. In-process ordering: for events e, f in the same process pip_ipi​﻿ if e→ife\xrightarrow{\text{i}}fei​f﻿ then e→HBfe\xrightarrow{\text{HB}}feHB​f﻿
  1. asynch communication: for any event e=send(m) (non-blocking) and f=receive(m) then e→HBfe\xrightarrow{\text{HB}}feHB​f﻿
  1. Sych communication: e = send(m), f = receive(m) then:
    1. for any events g such that e→HBge \xrightarrow{\text{HB}} geHB​g﻿ then f→HBgf \xrightarrow{\text{HB}} gfHB​g﻿
    1. for any events h such that f→HBhf \xrightarrow{\text{HB}} hfHB​h﻿ then e→HBhe \xrightarrow{\text{HB}} heHB​h﻿

Strong HB

  • if e→ob(V)fe\xrightarrow{\text{ob}(V)} feob(V)​f﻿

Weak HB

Consider only the precedence of a read op. wrt. the previous write

  • The version number of a variable V is incremented at any write op.
  • v(V,e)v(V, e)v(V,e)﻿ indicates the version number of V immediatly after e (write)

  1. For a write events e and a read event f on the same V, if v(V,e)=v(V,f)v(V, e) = v(V, f)v(V,e)=v(V,f)﻿ then e→HBfe\xrightarrow{\text{HB}}f eHB​f﻿

Events and Local States

Events are something that change the internal state of the program

  • A local computation corresponds to a sequence of local states, with transitions triggered by events.

We can define HB′HB'HB′﻿ that is HB but with reflexivity (event e happens before itself)

Then we can state σia→σσjb ≐eia+1→HB’ejb\sigma_i^a \xrightarrow{\sigma} \sigma_j^b \space \doteq e_i^{a+1} \xrightarrow{\text{HB'}} e_j^bσia​σ​σjb​ ≐eia+1​HB’​ejb​﻿

Global States

A distributed execution can be modeled as a partial order on the set of all states S: (S,→σ)S: \space (S, \xrightarrow{\sigma})S: (S,σ​)﻿

A global states is a collection of one local state per process:

A GS is consistent if: σi∣∣σj ∀i,j, i≠j\sigma_i || \sigma_j \space \forall i, j, \space i \neq jσi​∣∣σj​ ∀i,j, i=j﻿

A sequential observation is a sequence of all events/states, that complies with their partial order (HB).

  • A sequential observation corresponds to a path in the reachability graph

Logical Clocks

If we need to deal with the relative orderings of event occurrences, we can substitute the “global time” with an index that relates to the ordering of events.

A logical clock C(⋅)C(⋅)C(⋅)﻿ is a means to map events onto a partial order, so that if e→HBfe \xrightarrow{\text{HB}} feHB​f﻿ implies

C(e)<C(f)C(e) < C(f)C(e)<C(f)﻿ (clock consistency property)

  • The simplest co-domain for C(⋅)C(⋅)C(⋅)﻿: sequence of increasing integers. In this case, the corresponding time can be said linear time.

Lamport Timestamps

A classical logical clock TLpT_{Lp}TLp​﻿ : an event e is associated with the length of the longest HB chain to reach e.

  • presented just for the simple model with asynch communication, can be extended for shared variables and synch communication

Each process pip_ipi​﻿ keeps a local counter clockiclock_iclocki​﻿. Initialized to 0 and then updated with the following rules:

  1. For all the events but receives clocki←clocki+1 clock_i \leftarrow clock_i + 1 clocki​←clocki​+1 ﻿and then: TLp(e)←clockiT_{Lp}(e) \leftarrow clock_iTLp​(e)←clocki​﻿
  1. On send events, its value is piggybacked in msg m (added)
  1. With receives clocki←max⁡(clocki,ts(m))+1clock_i \leftarrow \max(clock_i, ts(m)) + 1clocki​←max(clocki​,ts(m))+1﻿ and then TLp(e)←clockiT_{Lp}(e) \leftarrow clock_iTLp​(e)←clocki​﻿
  • p1p_1p1​﻿ has no receive events so its normal counted

Properites of Lamport Timestamps

  1. clock consistency property: e→HBfe \xrightarrow{\text{HB}} feHB​f﻿ implies TLp(e)<TLp(f)T_{Lp}(e) < T_{Lp}(f)TLp​(e)<TLp​(f)﻿ → by construnction
  1. If TLp(e)≤TLp(f)T_{Lp}(e) \leq T_{Lp}(f)TLp​(e)≤TLp​(f)﻿ either e happened before f or e∣∣fe||fe∣∣f﻿ (by contraposition of the above)
  1. If TLp(e)=TLp(f)T_{Lp}(e) = T_{Lp}(f)TLp​(e)=TLp​(f)﻿ then e∣∣fe||fe∣∣f﻿ (applying two times the above relation)

Totally ordered Lamport Timestamps

I can defined the total order TLtT_{Lt}TLt​﻿ over all the events in a way consistent with HB relation.

  • when I have to order the events but have the same timestamp

For process pip_ipi​﻿, the totally ordered clock can be defined as the pair TLt=(TLp,i)T_{Lt} = (T_{Lp}, i)TLt​=(TLp​,i)﻿

  • (a,b)<(c,d)  ⟺  (a<c)∨((a=c)∧(b<d))(a, b)<(c, d) \iff (a<c) \lor ((a=c)\land(b<d))(a,b)<(c,d)⟺(a<c)∨((a=c)∧(b<d))﻿
  • Otherwise I can shift the logical clock by B+iB+iB+i﻿ bits with B=log2nB = log_2nB=log2​n﻿ (parte alta)

Strong Clock Consistency

I want e→HBf  ⟺  C(e)<C(f)e \xrightarrow{\text{HB}} f \iff C(e) < C(f)eHB​f⟺C(e)<C(f)﻿

I need to keep a vector counter ViV_iVi​﻿ of n integers at each process pip_ipi​﻿

  • Vi[j]V_i[j]Vi​[j]﻿ corresponds to the most recent value of Vj[j]V_j[j]Vj​[j]﻿ as detected by pip_ipi​﻿ → the number of events on pjp_jpj​﻿ that could have influenced pip_ipi​﻿
  • whenever pip_ipi​﻿ sends a message the most recend value of the vector timer is piggybacked in the message
  • I will have a vector timestam TV(e)T_V(e)TV​(e)﻿

Rules

  1. ∀e Vi[i]←Vi[i]+1\forall e \space V_i[i] \leftarrow V_i[i]+1 ∀e Vi​[i]←Vi​[i]+1﻿
  1. On send events TV(e)=ts(m)T_V(e)=ts(m)TV​(e)=ts(m)﻿ is piggybacked in msg m
  1. On receive events, Vi←maxcomp_wise(Vi,ts(m))V_i \leftarrow max_{\text{comp\_wise}}(V_i, ts(m))Vi​←maxcomp_wise​(Vi​,ts(m))﻿
  1. Finally TV(e)←ViT_V(e) \leftarrow V_iTV​(e)←Vi​﻿

Properties

  • at least one element in a particular position different on the two vectors
  • They are uniquely associented with the events. If two timestamps are equal then the events are the same

Strong Clock-Consistency: TV(e)<TV(f)T_V(e) < T_V(f)TV​(e)<TV​(f)﻿ then e→HBfe \xrightarrow{HB} feHB​f﻿

Proof:

  1. By contraposition, let's show ¬(e→HBf) \neg(e \xrightarrow{HB} f)¬(eHB​f)﻿ implies TV(e)≮TV(f)T_V(e) \not< T_V(f)TV​(e)<TV​(f)﻿
  1. TV(e)≮TV(f)T_V(e) \not< T_V(f) TV​(e)<TV​(f)﻿ means that, for at least one position i, TV(e)[i]>TV(f)[i]T_V(e)[i] > T_V(f)[i]TV​(e)[i]>TV​(f)[i]﻿
  1. Say e is in pip_ipi​﻿, and f in a different pjp_jpj​﻿. Just before e, pip_ipi​﻿ increases its Vi[i]V_i[i]Vi​[i]﻿, say to value ttt﻿, thus TV(e)[i]=tT_V(e)[i] = tTV​(e)[i]=t﻿.
  1. As ¬(e→HBf)\neg(e \xrightarrow{HB} f)¬(eHB​f)﻿, there is no way for value t to propagate to pj p_jpj​﻿, thus TV(f)[i]<tT_V(f)[i] < tTV​(f)[i]<t﻿

Let F(C)={f1,…,fn}F(C) = \{f_1, \dots , f_n\}F(C)={f1​,…,fn​}﻿ be the set of events in the frontier of a cut CCC﻿.

Let the cut timestamps to be: TV(C)=maxcomp_wise(TV(f1),…,TV(fn))T_V(C)= max_{comp\_wise}(T_V(f_1), \dots , T_V(f_n))TV​(C)=maxcomp_wise​(TV​(f1​),…,TV​(fn​))﻿
